translations.text: These are the names of the sons of Israel who entered the land of Egypt with their father Jacob. Each came with his household.
Reuben, Simeon, Levi, and Judah;
Issachar, Zebulun, and Benjamin;
Dan, Naphtali, Gad, and Asher.
Joseph was already in the land of Egypt. All the people descended from Jacob numbered seventy-five.
Joseph died, as did all his brothers and that entire generation.
The Israelites multiplied and became numerous and prolific. They grew exceedingly strong, and the land was filled with them.
Another king rose to power over Egypt who did not know Joseph.
He said to the people, “Look, the Israelite people are mighty and numerous, and they are stronger than we are.
Come, let us deal shrewdly with them, for as they multiply, if war comes upon us, they too will join our enemies, fight against us, and leave our land.”
He appointed overseers of forced labor over them to oppress them with work. They built fortified cities for Pharaoh: Pithom, Rameses, and On, which is the City of the Sun.
The more they oppressed them, the more they multiplied and grew strong. The Egyptians treated the Israelites harshly.
The Egyptians subjected the Israelites to painful slavery.
They made their lives miserable with hard labor, with bricks and mortar, with every kind of work in the fields, and with all the work they cruelly forced them to do.
The king of Egypt spoke to the Hebrew midwives. One was named Shiphrah, and the other was named Puah.
He said to them, “When you help the Hebrew women give birth, when the time for delivery comes, if the child is a boy, kill him; but if it is a girl, deliver her.”
Those midwives feared God and did not do as the king of Egypt had commanded them. They kept the boys alive.
The king of Egypt summoned the midwives and said to them, “Why do you act this way and keep the boys alive?”
The midwives said to Pharaoh, “The Hebrew women are not like the Egyptian women. They give birth before the midwife comes.”
God treated the midwives well, and the people became numerous and grew very strong.
Because the midwives feared God, they built houses.
Pharaoh commanded all his people, saying, “Throw every boy born to the Hebrews into the Nile, but keep every girl alive.”
There was a man from the tribe of Levi who took a woman from the daughters of Levi as his wife.
(He lived with her.) She conceived and gave birth to a boy. When they saw that he was beautiful, they kept him for three months.
When they could no longer hide him, his mother took a basket and coated it with bitumen and pitch. She put the child inside it and placed it among the reeds beside the Nile.
His sister watched from a distance to find out what would happen to him.
Pharaoh’s daughter went down to bathe in the river, and her servant girls walked along the river. When she saw the basket on the riverbank, she sent her servant girl, who brought it.
She opened it and saw a child crying inside the basket. Pharaoh’s daughter had pity on him and said, “This child is one of the Hebrew women’s children.”
The child’s sister said to Pharaoh’s daughter, “Would you like me to call a nursing woman from among the Hebrew women to nurse this child for you?”
Pharaoh’s daughter said to her, “Go.” The girl came and called the child’s mother.
Pharaoh’s daughter said to her, “Look after this child for me and nurse him for me, and I will pay you your wages.” The woman took the child and nursed him.
When the child had grown, she took him to Pharaoh’s daughter, and he became her son. She named him Moses, saying, “Because I drew him out of the water.”
After many days had passed, Moses grew up and went out to his brothers. He saw their suffering and found an Egyptian man beating a Hebrew, one of his brothers, the children of Israel.
He looked this way and that, and when he saw no one, he killed the Egyptian and buried him in the sand.
He went out on the second day and found two Hebrew men fighting. Moses said to the one doing wrong, “Why are you beating your fellow man?”
He said to him, “Who appointed you ruler and judge over us? Do you want to kill me as you killed the Egyptian yesterday?” Moses was afraid and said, “Has this matter become known like this?”

[Pharaoh heard about this matter,] and (Pharaoh) wanted to kill Moses. Moses fled from Pharaoh’s presence and lived in the land of Midian. When he reached a place in the land of Midian, he sat beside a well.
The priest of Midian had seven daughters, who tended their father’s sheep. When they came, they drew [?] until they filled the troughs to water their father’s sheep.
When the shepherds came, they drove the women away. Moses stood up, rescued them, and watered the sheep.
They went to their father Reuel, and he said to them, “How have you come back so quickly today?”
They said to him, “An Egyptian man rescued us from the shepherds. He drew water for us and watered our sheep.”
He said to his daughters, “Where is he? Why did you leave the man like that? Call him so that he may eat some food.”
Moses stayed with that man, and he gave Moses his daughter Zipporah to be his wife.

The woman conceived and bore a son. Moses named him Gershom, saying, “Because I am a stranger in a foreign land.” (He fathered another son and named him Eliezer, saying, “The God of my father, my helper, rescued me from Pharaoh’s hand.”)
After many days, the king of Egypt died. The children of Israel groaned because of their labor and cried out, and their cry because of their labor rose to God.
God heard their groaning, and God remembered his oath to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
God looked upon the children of Israel and made himself known to them.
Moses was tending the sheep of Jethro, his father-in-law, the priest of Midian. He took his sheep into the wilderness and reached Horeb, the mountain of God.
The angel of God appeared to Moses in a flame of fire from a bush. Moses saw that fire was burning from the bush, but the bush was not being burned up.
Moses said, “I will go over and look at this great sight, to see why this bush is not being burned up.”
When the Lord saw that he had come to look, the Lord called to him from the bush and said, “Moses, Moses!” He said, “What is it?”
He said to him, “Do not come near here. Take your sandals off your feet, because the place where you are standing is holy ground.”
He said to him, “I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.” Moses turned his face away because he was afraid to look upon God.
The Lord said to Moses, “I have indeed seen the suffering of my people who are in Egypt. I have heard their cry because of the taskmasters, and I know their distress.

I have come down to rescue them from the hand of Egypt and bring them into a good and spacious land, to bring them out of that land into a land flowing with milk and honey, into the territory of the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites, Girgashites, and Jebusites.
And now, look, the groaning of the children of Israel has reached me, and I have seen the suffering with which the Egyptians afflict them.
Now come. I will send you to Pharaoh, king of Egypt, and you will bring my people, the children of Israel, out of the land of Egypt.”
Moses said to God, “Who am I that I should go to Pharaoh, king of Egypt, and bring the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt?”
The Lord said to him, “I will be with you. This will be the sign to you that I have sent you: when you have brought my people out of the land of Egypt, you will serve God on this mountain.”
Moses said to God, “Look, I will go to the Israelites and tell them, ‘The God of your ancestors has sent me to you.’ If they ask me his name, what shall I tell them?”
God said to him, “I am the one who exists.” He said to him, “This is what you shall say to the Israelites: ‘The one who exists has sent me to you.’”

God also said to Moses, “This is what you shall say to the Israelites: ‘The Lord, the God of your ancestors, has sent me to you.’ This is my name forever, and this is how I am to be remembered from generation to generation.”

“Come and gather your leaders, the leaders of the Israelites, and say to them, ‘The Lord, the God of your ancestors, has appeared to me—the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob—saying, “I have surely watched over you concerning everything that has happened to you in the land of Egypt.”’

“And I said, ‘I will take you out of the suffering of Egypt and bring you up into the land of the Canaanites, Hittites, Hivites, Amorites, Perizzites, Girgashites, and Jebusites, into a land flowing with milk and honey.’

“They will listen to your voice. You and the elders of Israel shall go to the king of Egypt and say to him, ‘The Lord, the God of the Hebrews, has called us. So let us go a three-day journey into the wilderness to offer sacrifices to the Lord our God.’
“I know that Pharaoh, the king of Egypt, will not allow you to leave except under the force of a mighty hand.
“I will stretch out my hand and kill the Egyptians with all the wonders that I will perform among them. After that, he will let you go.
“I will give this people favor in the sight of the Egyptians, and when you leave, you will not go out empty-handed.

“Instead, each woman shall borrow silver and gold articles and clothing from her neighbor and from the woman staying in her house. Put them on your sons and daughters, and you shall plunder the Egyptians.”
Moses answered and said, “But if they do not believe me or listen to my voice, and say to me, ‘The Lord has not appeared to you,’ what shall I say to them?”
The Lord said to Moses, “What is this in your hand?” He said, “A staff.”
He said to him, “Throw it on the ground.” He threw it on the ground, and it became a snake, and Moses fled from it.
The Lord said to Moses, “Stretch out your hand and take it by the tail.” Moses stretched out his hand and took it by the tail, and it became a staff in his hand.
He said to him, “This is so that they may believe you, that the Lord, the God of their ancestors—the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob—has appeared to you.”

The Lord again said to Moses, “Put your hand inside your robe.” He put his hand inside his robe. He said to him, “Take your hand out of your robe.” He took his hand out of his robe, and it was entirely white with leprosy.

He said to him again, “Put your hand inside your robe.” He put his hand inside his robe. Again he said to him, “Take your hand out of your robe.” He took his hand out of his robe, and it returned to the color of his flesh.
He said to him, “If they do not believe you or listen to your voice because of the first sign, they will believe the message of the second sign.
“If they do not believe these two signs or listen to your voice, take some water from the Nile and pour it onto dry ground. The water you take from the Nile will become blood on the dry ground.”
Moses said to the Lord, “I beg you, Lord! I have had no eloquence, either before or in the past, nor since I, your servant, began to speak. I am poor in speech and slow of tongue.”
The Lord said to Moses, “Who gave human beings a mouth? Who makes someone mute or deaf, sighted or blind? Is it not I, the Lord God?”
“Now go, and I will open your mouth and teach you what you must say.”
He said, “I beg you, Lord! Find someone else who is capable, whom you can send.”

The Lord's anger flared against Moses, and he said to him, “Is not Aaron the Levite your brother? I know that he can certainly speak for you. Look, he is coming out to meet you; he will see you and rejoice.
“You shall speak to him and put my words in his mouth. I will open your mouth and his mouth, and I will teach you what you shall do.”
He will speak for you to the people. He will be your mouth, and you will act for him in matters concerning God.
Take this staff in your hand; with it you will perform signs.

Moses went and returned to Jethro, his father-in-law, and said to him, “Let me go back to my brothers who are in the land of Egypt and see whether they are still alive.” Jethro said to Moses, “Go in peace.” After many days, the king of Egypt died.
God said to Moses in the land of Midian, “Rise and go to the land of Egypt, for all those who were seeking your life have died.”
Moses took his wife and his children, put them on donkeys, and returned to the land of Egypt. Moses took in his hand that staff which came from God.

God said to Moses, “As you go back to the land of Egypt, remember all the wonders I have placed in your hands, so that you perform them before Pharaoh. But I will harden his heart, and he will not let the people go.”
You shall say to Pharaoh, “This is what the Lord says: Israel is my firstborn son.
I tell you, ‘Let my people go so that they may serve me.’ But you have refused to let them go. Know, then, that I will kill your firstborn son.”
On the journey, at a lodging place, the angel of the Lord met him and wanted to kill him.
Zipporah took a razor and cut off her son’s foreskin. She fell at his feet and said, “Let this blood from my son’s circumcision be a substitute for him.”
Then he withdrew from him, because she said, “Let this blood from my son's circumcision be a substitute for him.”
The Lord said to Aaron, “Go into the wilderness to meet Moses.” He went, met him at the mountain of God, and kissed him.
Moses told Aaron all the words of the Lord who had sent him, and all the signs he had commanded him to perform.
Moses and Aaron went and gathered all the elders of the Israelites.
Aaron told them all the words that God had spoken to Moses, and he performed the signs before the people.
The people believed and rejoiced because God had visited the Israelites and had seen their suffering. The people bowed their heads and worshiped.
After this, Moses and Aaron went in to Pharaoh and said to him, “This is what the Lord, the God of Israel, says: Let my people go so that they may celebrate my festival in the wilderness.”
Pharaoh said, “Who is he, that I should obey his voice and let the Israelites go? I do not know the Lord.” And he would not let Israel go.
They said to him, “The God of the Hebrews has called us. Let us go, then, on a three-day journey into the wilderness to sacrifice to the Lord our God, so that death and slaughter do not overtake us.”
The king of Egypt said to them, “Moses and Aaron, why are you keeping these people from their work? Go back to your work.”
Pharaoh said to them, “Look, the people of the land are now numerous and fill the land. [?] give them rest from their work.”
Pharaoh gave orders to the people's taskmasters and to the scribes, saying to them:
“From now on, do not give the people straw for making bricks as you did in former days. Let them go and gather straw themselves.
They must make the same quota of bricks every day. You must not reduce it for them at all; rather, increase it, for they are idle. They cry out and say, ‘Let us go and sacrifice to the Lord our God.’
Make the work heavier for these people, so that they think about it and do not think about useless words.”
The people's taskmasters and the scribes drove them on and said to the people, “This is what Pharaoh says: We will no longer give you straw.
Go yourselves and gather straw wherever you find it. Nothing at all will be deducted from your quota.”
The people scattered throughout the whole land of Egypt to gather stubble for themselves in place of straw.
Their taskmasters kept urging them on, saying, “Complete your work each day, just as when we gave you straw.”
The record keepers of the Israelite tribes, whom Pharaoh’s officials had appointed over them, were beaten. They were asked, “Why have you not completed your quota of bricks today as you did before?”
The Israelites’ record keepers went to Pharaoh and cried out, saying, “Why do you treat your servants this way?”
“Your servants are given no straw, yet they are told, ‘Make bricks!’ Look, your servants are being beaten, and your people are being mistreated.”
He said to them, “You are idle and lazy! That is why you say, ‘Let us go and sacrifice to our God.’
“Now go and work. You will not be given straw, but you must deliver your quota of bricks.”
The Israelites’ record keepers saw that they were in trouble and said, “Our daily quota of bricks must not be reduced.”
They met Moses and Aaron as they were coming out from Pharaoh.
They said to them, “May the Lord look upon us and judge, because you have made us stink before Pharaoh and his officials, putting a sword in his hand with which to kill us.”
Moses returned to the Lord and said, “Lord, why have you brought suffering upon this people? Why did you send me?
“Ever since I went to Pharaoh to speak to him with your message, he has brought suffering upon your people, and you have not rescued this people.”
The Lord said to Moses, “Now you will see what I will do to Pharaoh. Under a mighty hand he will send them away, and under an uplifted arm he will drive them out of his land.”
God spoke to Moses and said to him, “I am the Lord,
“who appeared to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, for I am their God. But I did not make my name, the Lord, known to them.
“I established my oath with them to give them the land of Canaan, the land in which they lived.
“I have heard the outcry of the Israelites, whom the Egyptians enslave, and I have remembered my oath.
“Quickly tell the Israelites, ‘I am the Lord. I will bring you out from under the power of the Egyptians, rescue you from their slavery, and redeem you with an uplifted arm and great judgment.
“‘I will take you for myself and be your God. Then you will know that I am the Lord your God, who brings you out of the land of Egypt and from under the power of the Egyptians.
“‘I will bring you into the land that I stretched out my hand to swear I would give to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. I will give it to you as an inheritance. I am the Lord.’”
Moses told the Israelites this, but they did not listen to Moses because of their discouragement and the hardship of their work.
The Lord said to Moses:
“Go in and tell Pharaoh, king of Egypt, to send the Israelites out of his land.”
Moses spoke before the Lord and said, “Look, the Israelites have not listened to me. How will Pharaoh listen to me, when I cannot speak well?”
The Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron and commanded them to tell Pharaoh, king of Egypt, to bring the Israelites out of the land of Egypt.
These are the messengers, according to their ancestral houses:
The sons of Reuben, Israel’s firstborn, were Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron, and Carmi. These were Reuben’s descendants.
The sons of Simeon were Jemuel, Jamin, Ohad, Jachin, Zohar, and Shaul, whose mother was a Phoenician (Canaanite) woman. These were Simeon’s descendants.
These were the names of Levi’s sons according to their families: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari. Levi lived 137 years.
These are the sons of Gershon: Libni and Shimei, according to their ancestral households.
The sons of Kohath were Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel. Kohath lived 133 years.
The sons of Merari were Mahli and Mushi. These are the descendants of the house of Levi, according to their clans.
Amram took Jochebed, the daughter of his father's brother, as his wife. She bore him Aaron, Moses, and their sister Miriam. Amram lived 137 years.
The sons of Izhar were Korah, Nepheg, and Zichri.
The sons of Uzziel were Mishael, Elzaphan, and Zithri.
Aaron took Elisheba, the daughter of Amminadab and sister of Nahshon, as his wife. She bore him Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar.
The sons of Korah were Assir, Elkanah, and Abiasaph. These are Korah's descendants.
Eleazar, Aaron's son, took one of Putiel's daughters as his wife. She bore him Phinehas. This is the beginning of the genealogy of the Levites, according to their clans.
These are Aaron and Moses, whom the Lord told to bring the Israelites out of the land of Egypt with their forces.
These are the ones who spoke to Pharaoh, king of Egypt, so that he would bring the Israelites out of the land of Egypt. They are Moses and Aaron.
On the day when the Lord spoke to Moses in the land of Egypt, the Lord spoke to Moses and said to him, “I am the Lord. Tell Pharaoh, king of Egypt, everything that I tell you.”
Moses said to the Lord, “Look, I am unclean. How will Pharaoh listen to me?”
The Lord said to Moses, “Look, I have made you a god to Pharaoh, and your brother Aaron will be your prophet.”
“You must speak everything that I command you, and Aaron must tell Pharaoh to send the Israelites out of his land.
I will harden Pharaoh's heart and multiply my signs and wonders in the land of Egypt.
Pharaoh will not listen to you. I will lay my hand upon the land of Egypt and, by my power, bring my people, the Israelites, out of the land of Egypt with great punishment.
Then all Egypt will know that I am the Lord, when I stretch out my hand over the land of Egypt and bring the Israelites out from among them.”
Moses and Aaron did just as the Lord commanded them. That is what they did.
Moses was eighty years old and Aaron was eighty-three years old when they spoke to Pharaoh.
The Lord said to Moses and Aaron:
“If Pharaoh says to you, ‘Give us a sign and a wonder,’ tell your brother Aaron, ‘Take this staff and throw it down before Pharaoh and his officials, and it will become a snake.’”
Moses and Aaron went in before Pharaoh and did just as the Lord commanded them. Aaron threw down his staff before Pharaoh and his officials, and it became a snake.
Pharaoh summoned the wise men and the sorcerers, and the magicians of Egypt did the same as Moses and Aaron through their spells.
They threw down their staffs, and they became snakes. But Aaron's staff swallowed their staffs.
Pharaoh's heart hardened, and he refused to listen, just as the Lord had said.
The Lord said to Moses, “Pharaoh’s heart has become hard, so that he will not let the people go.”
“Go to Pharaoh in the morning. He is going out to the water and will stand there. Meet him on the bank of the Nile, and take in your hand the staff that became a snake.
Say to him, ‘The Lord, the God of the Hebrews, sent me to you, saying, “Let his people go so that they may serve him in the wilderness.” But until now you have not listened.
This is what the Lord says: “By this you will know that I am the Lord: I will strike the water in the Nile with this staff in my hand, and it will become blood.
The fish in the Nile will die, the Nile will stink, and the Egyptians will not be able to drink water from the Nile.”’”

The Lord said to Moses, “Tell Aaron, ‘Take your staff and stretch out your hand over the waters of Egypt, over their rivers, their canals, their pools, and all their reservoirs, and they will become blood.’” There was blood throughout the land of Egypt, even in wooden and stone containers.
Moses and Aaron did as the Lord had commanded them. Aaron raised his staff and struck the water in the Nile before Pharaoh and his officials, and the water in the Nile became blood.
The fish in the Nile died, the Nile stank, and the Egyptians could not drink water from the Nile. There was blood throughout the land of Egypt.
The magicians of Egypt did the same with their spells. Pharaoh’s heart remained hard, and he refused to listen to them, just as the Lord had said.
Pharaoh turned back and went into his house, and even this did not stir his heart.
All the Egyptians dug around the Nile to get drinking water, because they could not drink water from the Nile.
Seven days passed after the Lord struck the Nile.
The Lord said to Moses, “Go in to Pharaoh and tell him, ‘This is what the Lord says: Let my people go so that they may serve me (in the wilderness).’”
“If you refuse to let them go, I will strike all your territory with frogs.

The Nile will spew out frogs. They will come up and enter your house, the inner rooms of your palace, and your bed, and the houses of your officials. They will come upon your people and into your dough and your ovens.
The frogs will climb onto you, your people, and your officials.”
The Lord said to Moses, “Tell Aaron your brother, ‘Stretch out the staff in your hand over the rivers, the canals, and the pools, and bring out frogs.’”
Aaron stretched out his hand over the waters of Egypt and brought out the frogs. The frogs came up and covered the land of Egypt.
The magicians did the same with their spells and brought frogs out over the land of Egypt.
Pharaoh summoned Moses and Aaron and said to them, “Pray to the Lord for me, so that he will remove the frogs from me and my people. I will let the people go, and they will sacrifice to the Lord.”

Moses said to Pharaoh, “Set a time for me to pray for you, your officials, and your people, so that the frogs will be destroyed from among you and your people and from your houses. They will remain only in the Nile.”
Pharaoh said to him, “Tomorrow.” He replied, “Very well, it will be as you say, so that you will know that there is no other besides the Lord.
The frogs will be removed from you, your houses, your officials, and your people. They will remain only in the Nile.”
Moses and Aaron left Pharaoh and cried out to the Lord for the destruction of the frogs, as Pharaoh had requested.
The Lord did as Moses said, and the frogs died in the houses, the towns, and the fields.
They gathered them into heaps, and the land stank.
When Pharaoh saw that there was relief, his heart became hard, and he refused to listen to them, as the Lord had said.
The Lord said to Moses, “Tell Aaron, ‘Stretch out the staff in your hand and strike the dust of the ground, and gnats will come out upon people and animals throughout the land of Egypt.’”
Aaron stretched out the staff in his hand and struck the dust of the ground. Lice came out upon people and animals. Lice came out of all the dust of the ground throughout the land of Egypt.
The magicians did the same with their spells to bring out lice, but they could not. The lice came upon people and animals.
The magicians said to Pharaoh, “This is the finger of God.” But Pharaoh’s heart remained hard, and he refused to listen to them, just as the Lord had said.
The Lord said to Moses, “Go in the morning and stand before Pharaoh. He is going out to the water. Say to him, ‘This is what the Lord says: Let my people go so that they may serve me.’”

If you refuse to let my people go, look, I will send dog flies upon you, your officials, your people, and your houses. The houses of Egypt will be filled with dog flies, as will the ground where they live.
On that day I will set apart the land of Goshen, where my people live, and there will be no dog flies there, so that you may know that I am the Lord of all the earth.
I will make a distinction between my people and your people. This will happen tomorrow.
And the Lord did so. Dogflies came in great numbers into Pharaoh’s houses, into the houses of his officials, and throughout the land of Egypt. The land was ruined by the dogflies.
Pharaoh summoned Moses and Aaron and said to them, “Go and offer sacrifices to your God in this land.”

Moses said to him, “We cannot do that, because what we sacrifice to our God is something the Egyptians consider forbidden. If we sacrifice what the Egyptians consider forbidden before their eyes, they will stone us.”
We will go three days’ journey into the open country and sacrifice to the Lord our God, as he told us.
Pharaoh said to him, “I will let you go to offer sacrifices to the Lord your God in the wilderness. But do not [?], and do not go far away. Pray to the Lord for me.”

Moses said to him, “Look, I am leaving you, and I will pray to the Lord. Tomorrow the dog flies will depart from Pharaoh and his officials. But do not act deceitfully again by refusing to let the people go to offer sacrifices to the Lord.”
Moses left Pharaoh and prayed to the Lord.
The Lord did as Moses had said and removed the dog flies from Pharaoh, his officials, and his people. Not a single one remained.
But Pharaoh hardened his heart this time also and refused to let the people go.
The Lord said to Moses, “Go to Pharaoh and tell him, ‘This is what the Lord, the God of the Hebrews, says: Let my people go so that they may serve me.
If you refuse to let my people go and continue to hold them firmly,
look, the hand of the Lord will come upon your livestock and your fields, upon the horses, donkeys, camels, cattle, and sheep, bringing very great death.
I will make a distinction between the livestock of Egypt and the livestock of Israel. Nothing belonging to the Israelites will die.’”
The Lord appointed a time and said, “Tomorrow the Lord will do this in the land.”
The Lord did this the next day, and all the livestock of Egypt died. But not one of the Israelites’ livestock died.
When Pharaoh saw that not one of the Israelites’ livestock had died, his heart became hard, and he did not let the people go.
The Lord said to Moses and Aaron, “Take handfuls of ashes from a furnace, and let Moses scatter them toward the sky in front of Pharaoh and his officials.”
It will become dust throughout the land of Egypt, and it will cause boils that break out on people and animals, on human beings and four-footed creatures throughout the land of Egypt.
They took ashes from a furnace in front of Pharaoh, and Moses scattered them toward the sky. They became erupting boils on people and animals.
The magicians could not stand before Moses because of the boils, for the boils afflicted the magicians and the whole land of Egypt.
The Lord hardened Pharaoh’s heart, and he did not listen to them, just as the Lord had told Moses.
The Lord said to Moses, “Go in the morning and stand before Pharaoh. Tell him, ‘This is what the Lord, the God of the Hebrews, says: Let my people go so that they may serve me.
For now, at this time, I will send all my plagues into your heart and upon your officials and your people, so that you may know that there is no one like me in all the earth.
Now I will stretch out my hand and strike you and your people. I will kill you, and you will be wiped from the earth.
But I have preserved you for this purpose: to show my power through you and to make my name known throughout all the earth.
Yet you still hold my people firmly and do not let them go.
Look, tomorrow at this time I will rain down very heavy hail, such as has never occurred since the land of Egypt was founded until this day.
Now hurry and gather in your livestock and everything you have in the field, because the hail will fall on every person and animal found in the field that has not entered a house, and they will die.
Those among Pharaoh’s officials who feared the word of the Lord gathered their livestock into houses.
But those who paid no attention in their hearts to the word of the Lord left their livestock in the open country.
And the Lord said to Moses, “Stretch out your hand toward heaven, and let hail fall throughout the land of Egypt, on people, on animals, and on all the vegetation in the land.”
Moses stretched out his hands toward heaven, and the Lord sent thunder and hail. Fire raced over the earth, and the Lord rained hail on all the land of Egypt.
Fire blazed amid the hail, and the hail was extremely heavy and violent, such as had never occurred since peoples first came into being in the land of Egypt.
Throughout the land of Egypt, the hail killed people and animals. The hail destroyed all the vegetation in the open country and shattered all the trees in the fields.
Only in the land of Goshen, where the Israelites lived, did no hail fall.
Pharaoh sent for Moses and Aaron and said to them, “I have sinned this time. The Lord is righteous, but my people and I are wicked.
Please pray to the Lord, so that it may grow quiet and there may be no more thunder from the Lord, or hail, or fire. I will let you go and will not keep you here any longer.”

Moses said to Pharaoh, “When I leave the city, I will raise my hands to the Lord. The thunder will stop, and there will be no more hail or rain, so that you may know that the earth belongs to the Lord.
But as for you and your officials, I know that you have never feared the Lord.”
The flax and barley were ruined. The barley was struck before it formed ears, and the flax because it had produced seed.
But the wheat and peas were not struck, because they were ripe.
Moses left Pharaoh and went outside the city. He raised his hands to the Lord, and the thunder and hail stopped, and rain no longer fell on the earth.
When Pharaoh saw that the rain, hail, and thunder had stopped, he sinned again and hardened his heart, and his officials did so too.
Pharaoh’s heart became stubborn, and he did not let the Israelites go, just as the Lord had told Moses.
And the Lord said to Moses, “Go in to Pharaoh, for I have hardened his heart and the hearts of his officials, so that my signs may come upon them together.”
“And so that you may tell your children and your children’s children all the ways I made a mockery of Egypt, and the signs I performed among them, and you may know that I am the Lord.”

Moses and Aaron went in before Pharaoh and said to him, “This is what the Lord, the God of the Hebrews, says: ‘How long will you refuse to respect me and refuse to let my people go so that they may serve me?
If you refuse to let my people go, look, tomorrow at this time I will bring many locusts over all your territories.

They will cover the surface of the earth, so that you will not be able to see the ground. They will eat everything remaining in the land that the hail left behind, and they will eat every tree you have grown in the land.

They will fill your houses, your officials’ houses, and all the houses in the land of Egypt—something neither your fathers nor those before their grandfathers have ever seen, from the time they first came into being on earth until this day.’” Then they turned and went out from Pharaoh.
Pharaoh’s officials said to him, “How long will this trouble be upon us? Let the people go so that they may serve the Lord their God. Or do you want to learn that Egypt has been destroyed?”
And they summoned Moses and Aaron to Pharaoh, and he said to them (Pharaoh to Moses and Aaron), “Go and serve the Lord your God. But who exactly are those of you who will go?”
Moses said to him, “We will go with our young and our old, with our sons and daughters, and with our sheep and cattle, because it is a festival of the Lord our God.”
He said to them (Pharaoh to Moses and Aaron), “May the Lord be with you in this way! Look, I will let you go, and your possessions too. Know, then, that you are planning evil.”
“In this way the men may go and serve the Lord. What, then, are you seeking?” And they drove Moses and Aaron out of Pharaoh’s presence.

The Lord said to Moses, “Stretch out your hand over the land of Egypt, and let locusts come up over the land and eat all the vegetation of the land and all the fruit of the trees that the hail has left.”
Moses raised his staff toward heaven, and the Lord brought a south wind over the land all that day and all night, until morning. That south wind carried the locusts,

and brought them over the whole land of Egypt. They settled on all the mountains of Egypt in immense numbers. Never before had there been locusts like these, and never afterward would there be any like them.

They covered the surface of the land, and the land was devastated. They ate all the vegetation of the land and all the fruit of the trees that remained after the hail. Not a single green thing remained on the trees or among all the vegetation of the fields throughout the land of Egypt.
Pharaoh hurried to summon Moses and Aaron and said to them, “I have sinned before the Lord your God and against you.
Forgive my sin once more, just this time, and pray to the Lord your God that he may remove this death from me.”
Moses went out from Pharaoh’s presence and prayed to the Lord.
The Lord changed the wind to a strong wind from the sea. It carried away the locusts and swept them into the Red Sea. Not a single locust remained anywhere in the land of Egypt.
But the Lord hardened Pharaoh’s heart, and he did not let the Israelites go.
The Lord said to Moses, “Stretch out your hand toward heaven, and let there be darkness in the land of Egypt, darkness that can be felt.”
And Moses stretched out his hand toward heaven, and darkness and dust covered the whole land of Egypt for three days.
No one could see anyone else, and no one rose from his bed for three days. But all the Israelites had light wherever they were.
And Pharaoh summoned Moses and Aaron and said to them, “Go and serve the Lord your God, but leave your sheep and cattle behind. You may take your possessions with you.”
Moses said to Pharaoh, “No! You yourself must also give us sacrifices to offer to the Lord our God.”

Our livestock must also go with us, and we will leave nothing behind, because we will take some of them to sacrifice to the Lord our God. We do not know what service we must render to the Lord our God until we arrive there.
But the Lord hardened Pharaoh’s heart, and he refused to let the Israelites go.
Pharaoh said to Moses, “Go away from me! Watch yourself if you see my face again, for when I see you again, you will die.”
Moses said to him, “Very well! I will not appear before you again.”
The Lord said to Moses, “I will bring one more plague upon Pharaoh and upon Egypt. After that he will let you go from here. When he lets you go, he will drive you out completely.
Speak quietly in the ears of the people, and let each man borrow from another man, and each woman from another woman, articles of silver and gold and clothing.”
The Lord gave the people favor in the eyes of the Egyptians, and the Egyptians lent to them. Moses himself became a very great man in the eyes of the Egyptians, of Pharaoh, and of his officials.
Moses said, “This is what the Lord says: ‘At midnight I myself will enter the midst of Egypt.

Every firstborn in the land of Egypt will die, from the firstborn of Pharaoh, who sits on the royal throne, to the firstborn of the slave woman who sits at the millstone, and all the firstborn of the livestock.
There will be a great cry throughout the land of Egypt, unlike any that has ever occurred or ever will occur again.
But not even a dog will lick any of the Israelites with its tongue, whether people or livestock, so that you may know how greatly the Lord is glorified among the Egyptians and among Israel.’
All these young men will come down to me and bow before me, saying, ‘Leave this land now, you and your people!’ After that I will leave.” And Moses went out from Pharaoh’s presence in anger.
The Lord said to Moses, “Pharaoh will not listen to you, so that I may multiply my signs and wonders in the land of Egypt.”
Moses and Aaron performed all the wonders before Pharaoh, but the Lord hardened Pharaoh’s heart, and he refused to let the Israelites leave the land of Egypt.
The Lord said to Moses and Aaron in the land of Egypt:
This month shall be the first of the months for you; put it before the other months of the year.
“Speak to the whole congregation of the Israelites and tell them: On the tenth day of this month, each man shall take a lamb for his family, one lamb for each household.
If the household is too small to finish one lamb, he shall share it with his neighbor, according to the number of people and how much each person can eat, so that they finish it.
Your lamb shall be a year-old male without blemish. You shall take a kid from the goats.
You shall keep it until the fourteenth day of this month, and the whole assembled congregation of the Israelites shall slaughter it toward evening.
They shall take some of its blood and put it on both doorposts and on the lintel of the house where they eat it.
They shall eat its meat that night, roasted over fire. You shall eat unleavened bread with bitter herbs.
Do not eat any of it raw or boiled in water, but roasted over fire, its head together with its legs.
You shall finish it and leave none of it until morning. You shall not break any of its bones. If any of it remains until morning, burn it in the fire.
You must eat it this way: with your belts fastened around your waists, your sandals on your feet, and your staffs in your hands. Eat it in haste, for it is the Lord’s Passover.
I will come into the land of Egypt that night and kill every firstborn in the land of Egypt, both human and animal. I will exact vengeance on all the gods of Egypt. I am the Lord.
This blood shall be a sign for you on the houses where you are. I will see the blood and protect you, and no destructive plague shall fall upon you when I bring it upon the land of Egypt.
This day shall be a memorial for you, and on it you shall celebrate a festival to the Lord throughout your generations. It shall be your festival as an everlasting ordinance.

You shall eat unleavened bread for seven days. On the first day, remove leaven from your houses. Whoever eats anything leavened from the first day through the seventh day shall be cut off from Israel.
The first day shall be designated holy, and the seventh day shall be holy for you. Do no ordinary work on those days. Only what must be prepared for each person to eat may be done for you.
Observe this commandment, for on this day I will bring your armies out of the land of Egypt. You shall celebrate this day throughout your generations as an everlasting ordinance.
Begin your observance on the fourteenth day of this first month. From that evening, eat unleavened bread until the evening of the twenty-first day of this month.
For seven days, no leaven shall be found in your houses. Whoever eats anything leavened shall be cut off from the congregation of Israel, whether a resident foreigner or someone born in your land.
Eat nothing leavened. In all your dwellings, eat unleavened bread.”
Moses summoned all the elders of Israel and said to them, “Go and take lambs for your families, and slaughter them for the Passover.

Take a bundle of hyssop and dip it in the blood beside the door. Apply some of that blood beside the door of the house to the lintel and both doorposts. And you must not leave that house until morning.

The Lord will come to kill the Egyptians. He will see the blood on the lintel and on both doorposts, and the Lord will pass over that doorway. He will not allow the killer to enter your houses to kill.
Observe this as an ordinance for yourselves and your children forever.
When you enter the land that the Lord will give you, as he said, observe this rite.
And when your children say to you, ‘What is this rite?’

You shall tell them, “This is the Passover sacrifice to the Lord, who protected the houses of the Israelites in the land of Egypt when he killed the Egyptians and saved our houses.” And the people bowed down and worshiped.
The Israelites went and did just as the Lord had commanded Moses and Aaron; that is what they did.

At midnight the Lord killed every firstborn in the land of Egypt, from the firstborn of Pharaoh, who sat on the royal throne, to the firstborn of the captive woman who drew water, and every firstborn of the livestock.
Pharaoh rose during the night, along with all his officials and all the Egyptians. There was a great cry throughout the land of Egypt, because there was no house without someone dead in it.
Pharaoh summoned Moses and Aaron during the night and told them, “Get up and leave my people, both you and the Israelites. Go and serve the Lord your God, as you said.
Take your sheep and your cattle too, and go. Bless me also.”
The Egyptians pressed the people of Israel to leave the land of Egypt quickly, because they said, “We will all die.”
The people took their dough before it had risen, with their dough wrapped in their clothes on their shoulders.
The Israelites did as Moses had commanded them and borrowed silver and gold articles and clothing from the Egyptians.
The Lord gave the people of Israel favor in the Egyptians’ eyes, and the Egyptians lent to them. Thus they plundered the Egyptians.
The Israelites traveled from Rameses to Succoth, six hundred thousand men on foot, besides those accompanying the baggage.
A large mixed group went up with them, along with sheep, cattle, and very many livestock.

They baked the dough they had brought out of Egypt and made it into unleavened flat cakes, because the Egyptians drove them out before they could let it rise. They could not stay and had not prepared provisions for their journey.
The time that the Israelites and their ancestors lived in the land of Egypt and the land of Canaan was four hundred and thirty years.
After four hundred and thirty years, all the Lord’s host left the land of Egypt at night.
It was a vigil kept by the Lord beforehand to bring them out of the land of Egypt. That same night is a vigil before the Lord, to be kept by all the Israelites throughout their generations.
And the Lord said to Moses and Aaron, “This is the law of the Passover: no one of a foreign people may eat of it.”
Every slave acquired by purchase shall be circumcised by you, and then he may eat some of it.
A resident alien or a hired worker shall not eat any of it.
It shall be eaten in one house. You shall not take any of that meat outside the house, and you shall not break its bones.
The whole congregation of Israel shall observe it.

If a foreigner comes to you and celebrates the Passover to the Lord, you shall circumcise all his males. Then he may approach and [?], and he shall be to you like a native of the land. No uncircumcised person shall eat any of it.
There shall be one law for the native and for the foreigner who comes to you.
The Israelites did just as the Lord had commanded Moses and Aaron; that is what they did.
And on that day the Lord brought the Israelites out of the land of Egypt with their forces.
And the Lord said to Moses:
Consecrate to me every firstborn, the first offspring to open any womb among the Israelites, whether human or animal. It belongs to me.

Moses said to the people, “Remember this day, on which you came out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery, because the Lord brought you out of here with a mighty hand. You shall not eat anything leavened.”
For on this day you are leaving, in the month of Hallelujah (Nisan).

And if the LORD brings you into the land of the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Hivites, Jebusites, Girgashites, and Perizzites, which he swore to give to your fathers, a land flowing with milk and honey, you shall remember this observance in this month.
For six days you shall eat unleavened bread, and the seventh day is a festival to the LORD.
You shall eat unleavened bread for seven days. No leavened bread shall be seen among you, and there shall be no leaven anywhere in your territory.
On that day you shall tell your son, saying, “This is because the Lord God did it—he did it for me when I came out of the land of Egypt.”
It shall be a sign on your hands and a reminder before your eyes, so that the LORD’s law may be in your mouth, for the LORD brought you out of Egypt with a strong hand.
You shall keep this law at its appointed time, from one day to the next.
And when the LORD brings you into the land of the Canaanites, which he swore to your fathers, and gives it to you,
you shall set apart for the LORD every male that opens the womb, born among your herds and your livestock.
Every firstborn donkey you shall exchange for a sheep. If you do not exchange it, you shall redeem it. And you shall redeem every firstborn male among your children.
And if your son asks you afterward, “What is this?” you shall tell him, “With a strong hand the LORD brought us out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.

When Pharaoh refused to let us go, he killed every firstborn in the land of Egypt, from the firstborn of humans to those of livestock. Because of this, I sacrifice to the LORD every male that opens the womb, and I redeem every firstborn among my children.”
It shall be a sign on your hand and something that does not depart from before your eyes, for the LORD brought us out with a strong hand.

When Pharaoh let the people go, the LORD did not lead them along the road through the land of the Philistines, although it was near, for the LORD said, “Perhaps they will change their minds when they see war and return to Egypt.”
The LORD led the people around by the wilderness road toward the Red Sea. And in the fifth generation the Israelites went up out of the land of Egypt.
Moses took Joseph’s bones with him, for Joseph had made the Israelites solemnly swear, saying to them, “When God surely comes to your aid, take my bones and bring them up with you from here.”
The Israelites journeyed from Succoth and camped at Etham, toward the wilderness.
The LORD led them by day in a pillar of cloud and by night in a pillar of fire.
The pillar of cloud by day and the pillar of fire by night did not depart from before all the people.
And the Lord said to Moses, “Tell the Israelites to turn back and camp opposite Pi-hahiroth, between Migdol and the sea, toward Baal-zephon. Camp opposite them, beside the sea.”
Pharaoh will say about the Israelites, “They are wandering in the land; the wilderness has trapped them.”
And I will harden Pharaoh’s heart, and he will pursue them. I will be glorified through Pharaoh and all his army, and all Egypt will know that I am the Lord.
And they did so.

And the king of Egypt was told that the people had fled. Pharaoh’s heart and the hearts of his officials turned against the people, and he said, “What have we done, letting the Israelites go so that they no longer serve us?”
Pharaoh mobilized all his chariots and gathered all his people with him.
He took seven hundred chosen chariots and all the horses of the Egyptians, with officers over them all.
The LORD hardened the heart of Pharaoh, king of Egypt, and he pursued the Israelites. But the Israelites were traveling with a raised hand.
The Egyptians pursued them and overtook them where they were encamped by the sea—all Pharaoh’s horses and chariots and his army—opposite Epaulis, toward Baal-zephon.
Pharaoh rose up, and the children of Israel looked and saw the Egyptians advancing behind them. They were very afraid, and the children of Israel cried out to the Lord.

And they said to Moses, “Was it because there were no graves in the land of Egypt that you brought us out to kill us in the wilderness? What have you done to us by bringing us out of the land of Egypt?”
Was this not what we told you in the land of Egypt: ‘Leave us alone so that we may serve the Egyptians’? For serving the Egyptians is better for us than dying in the wilderness.

Moses said to the people, “Have faith and stand firm, and you will see the deliverance from the Lord that he will accomplish for us today. For although you see the Egyptians today, you will never see them again, forever.”
The Lord will fight for you, and you must remain silent.
The Lord said to Moses, “Why do you cry out to me? Tell the children of Israel to drive their animals onward.”
But you, lift your staff and stretch out your hand over the sea and strike it, so that the children of Israel may enter the midst of the sea on dry ground.
Look, I will harden the heart of Pharaoh and of all the Egyptians, and they will enter after them. I will be glorified through Pharaoh, all his army, his chariots, and all his horses.
All the Egyptians will know that I am the Lord when I am glorified through Pharaoh, his chariot, and all his horses.
The angel of the Lord, who was going ahead of the camp of the children of Israel, moved away and stood behind them. The pillar of cloud also moved away from before them and stood behind them.
It came between the Egyptian camp and the Israelite camp. There was gloom and darkness, and they did not come together throughout the night.
Moses stretched out his hand over the sea and brought a strong south wind over the sea (over the sea) throughout the night. He made the sea dry ground and divided the water.
The children of Israel entered the midst of the sea on dry ground, and the water became a wall on their right and a wall on their left.
The Egyptians pursued them and entered after them. All Pharaoh’s horses, his chariots, and the riders entered the midst of the sea.
During the watch of the night just before dawn, the Lord looked into the Egyptian camp through the pillar of fire and cloud and issued a command against the Egyptian camp.
He bound the axles of their chariots and drove them with difficulty. The Egyptians said, “Let us flee from the Israelites, for the Lord is fighting for them.”
The Lord said to Moses, “Stretch out your hand over the sea, so that the water may return over the Egyptians, their chariots, and their riders.”

Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and the sea covered them that day and hemmed them in from behind. The Egyptians fled into the sea, and the Lord struck the Egyptians down in the midst of the sea.
The sea returned, and they were drowned with their chariots and their riders, along with all Pharaoh’s forces, as they entered the sea. Of all those who had entered, not one remained.
The children of Israel walked on dry ground in the sea, and the sea became a wall for them on their right and on their left.
The Lord saved Israel that day from the hands of the Egyptians, and Israel saw the Egyptians dead on the shore of the sea.
Israel saw the mighty power that the Lord had used against the Egyptians. The people feared the Lord and believed in the Lord, and they also honored Moses, the Lord’s messenger.

Moses and the children of Israel blessed the Lord with this blessing, saying: “Let us bless the Lord, for he is glorious, and praise is fitting for him. He threw the horse and its rider into the sea.”
My helper and protector has become my salvation. He is my God, and I will praise him; my father’s God, and I will exalt him.
The Lord crushes wars, and the Lord is his name.
He threw Pharaoh’s chariots and his army into the sea. Chosen men and riders in groups of three were drowned in the Red Sea.
The waves covered them, and they sank into the deep like a stone.
Your right hand, Lord, was glorified in power; your right hand, Lord, shattered the enemy.
In the greatness of your glory you crushed your enemies; you sent out your wrath, and it consumed them like straw.
At the blast of your wrath the water stood still; the water piled up like [?], and the waves froze in the middle of the sea.
The enemy said, “I will pursue and catch them; I will divide the plunder and satisfy myself. I will kill with my sword and subdue them with my hand.”
You sent out your wind, and the sea covered them; they sank like lead in the mighty waters.
Who among the gods is like you, Lord? Who is like you, glorified among the holy ones? Your glory is awesome, and you work wonders.
You stretched out your right hand, and the earth swallowed them.
And you led your people whom you redeemed; by your strength you made the remnant of your sanctuary rejoice.
The nations heard and trembled; anguish seized the inhabitants of Philistia.
At that time the chiefs of Edom trembled; shaking seized the messengers of Moab, and all the inhabitants of Canaan melted away.
Fear and trembling seized them; the strength of your arm was greater than rocks, until your people passed over, Lord, until your people passed over—this people whom you redeemed.
You brought them and planted them on the mountain of your sanctuary, in your prepared dwelling, Lord, which you made—the holy place, Lord, which your hands established.
The Lord will reign forever and forever and beyond.
For Pharaoh’s chariots went into the sea with his horses and riders, and the Lord brought the waters of the sea back over them. But the Israelites crossed on dry ground through the middle of the sea.
Miriam the prophetess, Aaron’s sister, took a tambourine in her hand, and all the women went out after her with tambourines and praise.
Miriam took the lead and said, “Let us bless the Lord. He is wonderful, wonderful! He threw the horse and its rider into the sea.”
Moses brought the Israelites out from the deep sea and led them into the wilderness of Shur. They traveled for three days through the wilderness and found no water to drink at Marah.
They could not drink at Marah because its water was bitter. For that reason, that place was called Bitter.
The people grumbled and said, “What shall we drink?”
Moses cried out to the Creator, and the Lord showed him a piece of wood. He threw it into the water, and the water became sweet. There he showed him righteousness and judgment, and tested him.

He said, “If you listen carefully to the voice of the Lord your Creator, do what is right before him, and heed the commandment he has given you, I will not send upon you any of the diseases that I brought upon the Egyptians. I am the Lord, your healer.”
They reached Elim, where there were twelve springs with pools and seventy palm shoots growing beside the waters.
They set out from Elim, and all the Israelites came into the wilderness of Sin, which is between Elim and Sinai, on the fifteenth day of the second month after they left the land of Egypt.
All the people of Israel grumbled against Moses and Aaron.

The Israelites said to them, “If only we had died by the Lord’s plague in the land of Egypt, when we sat beside the pots of meat and ate bread until we were full! You have brought us into this wilderness to kill all of us gathered here.”
The Lord said to Moses, “Look, I will send bread down from heaven for you. Let the people come and gather it each day, so that I may test whether they will follow my law or not.”
“On Friday they shall prepare what they bring in; it shall be twice what they regularly gather each day.”
Moses and Aaron said to all the people of Israel, “By evening you will know that the Lord brought you out of the land of Egypt.”
“In the morning you will see the Lord’s power, for the Lord has heard your grumbling. And who are we, that you grumble against us?”

Moses said, “In the evening the Lord will give you meat to eat, and in the morning bread until you are satisfied, because the Lord has heard your grumbling—the grumbling with which you grumble against us. And who are we? This grumbling of yours is not against us, but against the Creator.”
Moses said to Aaron, “Tell all the assembled Israelites, ‘Come before the Creator, for he has heard your grumbling.’”
While Aaron was speaking to all the assembled Israelites, they turned toward the wilderness, and the radiance of the Lord appeared in the cloud.
And the Lord said to Moses:

“I have heard the grumbling of the Israelites. Tell them, ‘In the evening you will eat meat, and in the morning you will have your fill of bread. Then you will know that I am the Lord, your Creator.’”
When evening came, quail came up and covered their whole camp. When morning came, dew lay around their camp.
Across the wilderness there was something fine, like coriander, and white like frost on the ground.
The Israelites saw it, and each said to the other, “What is this?” For they did not know. Moses said to them, “This is the bread the Lord has given you to eat.”
“This is what the Lord has said: Gather some of it in your vessels, each person according to the number of his people. Let each gather in his vessel for every person.”
The Israelites did so. Some gathered much, and some little.
They measured it with an omer. The one who had gathered much had no excess, and the one who had gathered little had no shortage. Each person gathered for his own household.
Moses said to the Israelites, “Do not leave any until tomorrow.”
They did not listen to Moses, and [?] until morning. It bred worms and stank, and Moses was angry with them.
They gathered it every morning, each for himself, and when the sun grew hot, it melted.
On Friday they gathered a double portion, two omers for each person. All the leaders of the assembly came and told Moses.
Moses said to them, “This is what Moses told them: Tomorrow is a Sabbath of rest, blessed to the Lord. Whatever you have to prepare, prepare, and whatever you have to cook, cook. Keep what remains.”
They kept it until morning, as Moses had commanded, and it did not stink, nor did worms appear in it.
Moses said to them, “Eat it today, because today is the Lord’s Sabbath. You will not find it in the wilderness.”
“For six days you shall gather it, but on the seventh day, the Sabbath, you will not find it.”
On the seventh day, some of the people went out to gather it, but found none.
The Lord said to Moses, “How long will you refuse to obey my commandments and my law?”
“See, the Lord has given you the Sabbath day. For this reason he has given you food for two days on Friday. Let everyone remain in his dwelling, and let no one leave his place on the Sabbath day.”
The people rested on the Sabbath day.
The Israelites called it manna. It was white, like coriander seed, and its taste was like a honey cake.

Moses said, “This is what the Lord commanded: Fill an omer with manna and keep it in your stores for your descendants, so that they may see the bread you ate in the wilderness when the Lord brought you out of the land of Egypt.”
Moses said to Aaron, “Take one thin sheet of gold, put an omer of manna in it, and set it before the Lord for your descendants in the days to come.”
For this is what the Lord commanded Moses, and Aaron placed it before the testimony to be kept.
The Israelites ate manna for thirty years, until they reached the land where he would settle them. They ate manna until they reached the border of Phoenicia.
An omer is a tenth part of three measures.
The whole camp of the Israelites set out from the wilderness of Sin, camp by camp, at the Lord’s command. They reached Rephidim, and there was no water there to drink.
The people quarreled with Moses and said to him, “Give us water to drink.” Moses said to them, “Why do you quarrel with me and put the Lord to the test?”
The people thirsted for water there. They grumbled against Moses and said to him, “Why did you bring us out of Egypt, to kill us, our children, and our livestock with thirst?”
Moses cried out to the Lord and said, “What shall I do with these people? A little more, and they will stone me.”
The Lord said to Moses, “Go ahead of the people, and take the elders of the people with you. Hold in your hand your staff, with which you struck the river.
Come to where I will stand nearby, at the rock of Horeb. Strike the rock, and water will come out of it, and the people will drink.” Moses did as the Lord commanded him, before the Israelites.
He named that place Testing and Dispute, because of the dispute that the Israelites raised and because they tested the Creator of all, saying, “Is the Lord with us or not?”
Amalek came and fought at Rephidim.
Moses said to Joshua, “Choose men for yourself, go out, and engage Amalek tomorrow. Look, I will stand on top of the hill with the staff of God in my hand.”
Joshua did as Moses commanded him and engaged Amalek. Moses, Aaron, and Hur went up to the top of the hill.
Whenever Moses raised his hands, Israel prevailed. Whenever Moses grew tired and lowered his hands, Israel was defeated.

Moses’ hands were heavy. They set a stone in place for him, and Aaron and Hur sat on them [?] and supported Moses’ hands, one on one side and one on the other. Moses’ hands remained raised until sunset.
Joshua routed Amalek and his people and killed them with the sword.
The Lord said to Moses, “Write this down as a memorial, and make it known to Joshua: I will utterly wipe out Amalek from under heaven.”
Moses built an altar to the Lord and named it Refuge,
because with a hidden hand the Lord will wage war against Amalek from generation to generation.
Jethro, the priest of Midian and Moses’ father-in-law, heard all that the Lord had done for Israel, his people, and that the Lord had brought Israel out of Egypt.
Jethro, Moses’ father-in-law, took Zipporah, Moses’ wife, after Moses had left her,
and his two sons. The name of one of Moses’ sons was Gershom, for he said, “I am a foreigner in a foreign land.”
The name of his other son was Eleazar, for he said, “My father’s Creator is my helper, and he rescued me from Pharaoh’s hand.”
Jethro, Moses’ father-in-law, came with Moses’ sons and wife to Moses in the wilderness, where they were camped at the foot of the mountain of God.
They told Moses, “Look, your father-in-law Jethro is coming to you, with your wife and both your sons.”
Moses went out to meet his father-in-law, greeted him, and kissed him. They greeted one another and went into the tent.
Moses told his father-in-law everything the Lord had done to Pharaoh and Egypt for Israel’s sake, all the suffering they had endured along the way, and how the Lord had rescued them.
Jethro was astonished at everything the Lord had done for them, rescuing them from the hand of Egypt and from the hand of Pharaoh.
Jethro said, “Blessed be the Lord, who rescued his people from the hand of Egypt and from the hand of Pharaoh.
Now I know that the Lord is greater than all gods, because on this account they were judged on their behalf [?].”

Jethro, Moses’ father-in-law, took an offering and made a sacrifice to the Lord in righteousness. Aaron and the leaders of the people of Israel came to eat bread with Moses’ father-in-law before the Lord.
On the next day, Moses sat to judge the people, and the people waited beside Moses from morning until evening.
Jethro saw everything he was doing for the people, and Jethro said to Moses, “What is this you are doing with the people? You sit alone, while all the people stand from morning until evening.”
Moses said to his father-in-law, “Because the people come to me to seek judgment from the Lord.”
When they have a dispute, they come to me, and I judge between them, explaining to each one God's judgments and his law.
Moses' father-in-law said to him, “What you are doing is not right. This is a great undertaking.
You and all the people with you will wear yourselves out. This matter is too burdensome for you, and you cannot do it alone.
Now listen to me, and I will advise you, and may God be with you. You yourself must represent the people before God and bring their cases before God.
Teach them God's commandments and his law, and show them the paths they should walk in and the work they should do.
You yourself must choose from all the people capable men, righteous men who hate arrogance, and appoint them as leaders over thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens.
Let them judge the people at all times. Let them bring you any case that is too difficult for them, but let them judge the simple cases themselves. They will lighten your burden and help you.
If you do what I say, God will strengthen you, and you will be able to judge, and these people will return to their homes in joy.”
Moses listened to his father-in-law's words and did as he told him.
Moses chose capable men from all Israel and appointed leaders among them over thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens.
They judged all the people at all times. They brought difficult cases to Moses, but decided the simple cases themselves.
Moses sent his father-in-law away to his own land, and he departed.
In the third month after the Israelites left the land of Egypt, on that day they came into the wilderness of Sinai.
They left Rephidim and reached the wilderness of Sinai, and Israel camped there opposite the mountain.
Moses went up the mountain of God. God called to Moses from the mountain and said to him, “Say this to the house of Jacob, and tell the children of Israel:
‘You have seen all that I did to the Egyptians, and how I carried you as on an eagle's wings and brought you to myself.
Now, if you listen to my voice and keep my commandments, you will be a righteous people belonging to me from among all peoples, for the whole earth is mine.
You will be a kingdom for me, people who offer sacrifices to me, a righteous people.’ Make these words known to the children of Israel.”
Moses came and called the elders of the people, and made known to them all these words that God had commanded them.
All the people answered with one voice and said, “We will do everything God has commanded us, and we will obey.” Moses brought the people's words up to God.
God said to Moses, “I will come to you in a pillar of cloud, so that the people may hear when I speak with you and may trust you forever and ever.” Moses made the people's words known to God.
God said to Moses, “Go down and instruct the people. Let them purify themselves today and tomorrow and wash their clothes.
Let them remain ready for the third day, because on the third day God will come down onto Mount Sinai in the sight of the people.
Set the people apart around it, and let them take care not to go up the mountain. Anyone who touches the mountain must be put to death.

Nor must they show their hands [?]. They must be stoned with stones or struck with missiles. Whether animal or human, they must not live. Once the sound of the trumpet and the cloud have passed from the mountain, they may go up the mountain.”
Moses went down from the mountain to the people and blessed them, and they washed their clothes.
He said to the people, “Be ready for the third day, and do not have sexual relations with women.”

On the third day you set out in the morning, and now you hear thunder, and there are lightning, clouds, and thick darkness on Mount Sinai, and a very loud trumpet blast. All the people in the camp trembled.
Moses brought the people out of the camp to meet the Creator, and they reached the mountain.
All of Mount Sinai was smoking because the Lord had descended upon it in fire. What came out of it was like smoke from a furnace, and all the people trembled greatly.
The trumpet sounded, growing louder and much stronger. Moses spoke, and God answered him with his voice.
The Lord descended onto Mount Sinai, onto the summit of the mountain, and Moses went up.
The Lord said to Moses, “Go down and warn the people not to approach the Lord to look at him, lest many among them fall.”
“Let the priests who approach the Lord God sanctify themselves, so that God does not destroy them.”
Moses said to the Lord, “The people cannot go up onto Mount Sinai, because you warned us and told us, ‘Do not touch the mountain, and keep it holy.’”
The Lord said to Moses, “Go down, and then come up, you and Aaron with you. But the priests and the people must not force their way up to the Lord, lest the Lord bring destruction among them.”
Moses went down to the people and spoke to them.
God spoke all these words, saying:
“I am the Lord God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of your slavery.
Do not worship gods other than me.
Do not make for yourself a god in the likeness of anything in heaven above, on the earth below, or in the waters beneath the earth.
Do not bow down to them or worship them, for I am the Lord your God. I am a jealous God, who punishes children for their father's sin, to the third and fourth generation of those who hate me.
But I show mercy to thousands who love me and keep my commandments, and to those who keep my law.
Do not swear falsely by the name of the Lord your Creator, for the Lord will not hold innocent anyone who uses his name falsely.
Remember the Sabbath day and keep it holy.
Work for six days, and do all your labor during them.
But the seventh day is a Sabbath to the Lord your God. Do not do any work on it—you, your son, your daughter, your donkey, any of your animals, or the foreigner who lives with you.
For in six days the Lord made heaven, earth, the sea, and everything in them, and he rested on the seventh day. Therefore the Lord blessed the seventh day and made it holy.
Honor your father and your mother, so that righteousness may be yours. You will have many days in the righteous land that the Lord God gives you.
Do not kill.
Do not commit adultery.
Do not steal.
False testimony: do not testify against your neighbor with false testimony.

Do not covet another man's wife. Do not covet another man's house, his fields, his male slave, his female slave, his cow, his oxen, or any of his animals—anything your neighbor has acquired as his possession.”
All the people saw the thunder and the flashes of lightning, heard the sound of the trumpet, and saw the mountain smoking. All the people were afraid and stood far away.
They said to Moses, “You speak with us, and let God speak with you, so that we do not die.”
Moses said to them, “God has come to you to test you, so that fear of him may remain upon you and you may not sin.”
The people stood far away, while Moses entered the thick darkness where God was.
God said to Moses, “Tell the house of Jacob and inform the children of Israel that I have spoken to you from heaven.”
Do not worship gods of silver, and do not worship gods of gold. Do not make such gods for yourselves.

“Make an altar of earth for me, and sacrifice on it your offerings and your redemption offerings, your sheep and cattle. In every place where I have named my name, I will come to you there and bless you.
“If you make me an altar of stone, do not build it with stones you have cut, for by putting your cutting tool upon it you have defiled it.
“Do not climb steps to my altar, so that your nakedness is not exposed there.”
These are also the ordinances they must observe.
If you acquire a Jewish slave, keep him for seven years, and in the seventh year set him free without payment.
If you acquired him alone, he shall leave alone. If you acquired him with his wife, he shall leave with his wife.
If his master gave him a wife and she bore him sons and daughters, his wife and children shall belong to his master, and he shall go free alone.
If your servant says, “I love my master, my mistress, my wife, and my children,” and does not want freedom,
his master shall take him to the court of the Creator's judges and bring him to the door at the threshold. His master shall pierce his ear with an awl, and he shall serve him forever.
If someone has given her in marriage, do not send her away as slave women are sent away.
If she does not please her master—she who trusted him—let him release her. He may sell her to another people, to a master wherever he wishes, because she herself consented.
If he wishes to give her to his son, he shall treat her as a daughter.
If he takes another woman for himself, he shall give her her food and clothing, and shall make a declaration to her that he will not shut her out.
If he does not do these three things for her, she shall leave him without paying a ransom.
If someone wounds another person and that person dies from his wound, the one who wounded him shall die.
If he wounded him unintentionally, and God delivered him into the right hand of the one who wounded him, I will show you a way where the killer may take refuge.
If someone plotted to kill his enemy and then took refuge, they shall take him from there and kill him.
Anyone who strikes his father or mother shall be sentenced to death.
If someone has stolen among the Israelites, and [?] your companion [?] you bring back [?], whoever you find shall be sentenced to death.
Anyone who curses his father or mother shall be sentenced to death.
If two men fight with each other and one wounds the other, whether with a stone or a stick, and confines him to bed—the one who wounded him having no hostility—
if he walks about outside despite his injury, using a staff, the one who wounded him shall be cleared. He shall pay him for his lost labor and pay the healer's fee.
If someone wounds his male or female slave with a rod and the slave dies, the one who inflicted the wound shall surely be put to death.
But if he survives one day and the second day, he will escape death [?], because he is his owner's money.
If two men fight and injure a pregnant woman, and she miscarries and there is no human form, they shall fine him if her husband agrees to a settlement, according to his demand.
If she miscarries when it is formed, he shall pay life for life.
An eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth, a hand for a hand, a foot for a foot.
Burn for burn, cut for cut, wound for wound.
If someone injures the eye of his male slave or his female slave and blinds it, he must set them free in compensation for their eye.
If he breaks a molar or tooth of his male or female slave, he shall set them free in compensation for their tooth.
If an ox gores a man or a woman and kills them, the ox must be stoned, and its flesh must not be eaten. The owner of the ox will be free from guilt.

But if his ox has been accustomed to goring in the past, and its owner has been warned but has not restrained it, and it kills a man or a woman, the ox must be stoned, and its owner must also be put to death.
If they demand a ransom for him, he must give a ransom for his life according to the amount agreed upon.
If it gores sons [?] ([?]) or daughters, he must pay what they assess.
Whether it is a male slave or a female slave, he shall give thirty pieces of silver to the slave’s owner in either case, and his ox shall be stoned.
If someone opens a pit or digs one and does not cover its opening, and an ox or a donkey falls into it,
the owner of the pit must make compensation, and he will take the carcass.
If an ox gores another person's ox and it dies, the owner of the ox must replace it for him. Otherwise, they must divide its price and their carcasses.
But if his ox has been accustomed to goring in the past, and he has been warned, he must give an ox in compensation for the ox, and he will take the carcass of the dead animal.
If someone steals an ox or a sheep and slaughters it, he must give five in place of one ox and four in place of one sheep.
If a thief is wounded while digging through and dies, the person who killed him will not be guilty of murder.
But if the sun has risen over the body, the person who killed him must die. If the thief has nothing, he must be sold in compensation for what he stole.
If they catch him and find what he stole in his possession, whether a donkey or a sheep, he must repay double.

If someone lets his animals feed in other people's fields or a vineyard, and lets them eat another person's fields, they must assess its produce, and he must make compensation. But if the animals consume the entire field while feeding, he must make compensation from the best of his field; if it is a vineyard, he must make compensation from the best of his vineyard.
If a fire breaks out and catches in the open country and burns a cultivated field or a heap of grain, the person who caused the burning must make compensation.
If someone entrusts silver or goods to another for safekeeping, and it is stolen from the person to whom it was entrusted, and the thief is found, the thief must repay double.
If the thief is not found, the householder must go before the Creator and swear concerning the deposit entrusted to him that he has neither misappropriated it nor concealed it.

Whether it is an ox, a donkey, or a sheep, whatever they claim from him concerning the deposit [?], whatever has happened, the matter between them must be settled there. The person who is at fault must repay double to the one who entrusted it to him.
If someone gives another person cattle or sheep, or any animal among them, and it dies or is injured or is carried off, and no one knows about it,
an oath before the Lord must stand between them that the custodian has not deliberately misappropriated it. On this account, the person entrusted with it need not make compensation.
But if what was entrusted to him is stolen, he must make compensation to the person who entrusted it to him.
If a wild animal seizes it in the open country, he must bring its carcass and need not make compensation.
If you borrow something from your neighbor and it is broken or dies, and the owner of the property is not there as guarantor, you must make compensation.
